content.title: Italy Curtails Ancestry-Based Citizenship Rights
content.text: 29 May 2025 As Italy enacts sweeping restrictions on citizenship by descent, millions of descendants of Italian immigrants, particularly in countries like Brazil and Argentina, find their ancestral ties to the homeland abruptly severed. Critics argued that the reform not only undermines Italy’s historic relationship with its diaspora but also sends a chilling message to foreign-born workers and communities who have long considered Italy part of their cultural identity. Parliament passes law ending great-grandparent claims On May 20th, Italy’s Lower House gave final approval to Decree-Law 36, with 137 votes in favor and 83 against. The law officially ends the right to claim Italian citizenship through great-grandparents. It now limits automatic recognition to two generations: only those with an Italian parent or grandparent born in Italy can apply. Even then, that ancestor must have exclusively held Italian citizenship at the time of death. Applicants must also prove legal residence in Italy for at least two years post-citizenship acquisition and before a child’s birth or adoption. If born abroad with dual nationality, a person will not automatically be considered Italian anymore. This change shuts the door on millions of descendants, especially those in Latin America, who grew up embracing their Italian roots. Reform as “betrayal” Outrage erupted across Italian communities abroad. Nicola Carè, a Democratic Party deputy representing Italians overseas, condemned the law as a “deep, painful and unjust wound” that weakens Italy’s connection with its global diaspora. “This is not reform,” Carè said during his speech in Parliament. “It is a step back. It limits transmission, restricts retroactivity, and empties the meaning of jus sanguinis.” Carè emphasized that the law punishes ordinary families, not opportunists seeking European Union (EU) passports. “Children and grandchildren of Italian emigrants will now be told, ‘You are not Italian enough to deserve your grandfather’s citizenship,’” he said. Marco Fedi, Chief Executive Officer of CO.AS.IT. and a former member of parliament, called the decree one of the worst betrayals in Italy’s history of relations with its global communities. “This reform is a bitter chapter for those who feel Italian, even if they were born far away,” Fedi wrote in an op-ed. He criticized the government for using an emergency decree under the pretense of national security to impose such sweeping changes. Policy “necessary” for integrity Italian Deputy Prime Minister Antonio Tajani defended the law, stating: “Being an Italian citizen is not a joke.” He condemned those using Italian passports merely for ease of travel, adding, “We want people to become Italian citizens because they feel connected to our country—not to shop in Miami.” The government argued that the reform brings order to an outdated system. It cited overuse and alleged abuse of ancestry claims, particularly by South Americans with Italian lineage. (Image courtesy of kieferpix via iStock) Brazil and Argentina hit hardest In 2023, over 61,000 people gained citizenship through ancestry. Brazilians accounted for a staggering 68.5%—more than 42,000 individuals. Argentinians followed, with over 16,000 becoming naturalized that year. These numbers reveal just how popular the jus sanguinis path has been outside Italy. Now, most of these applicants will no longer qualify. Instead, they must relocate to Italy and apply for residency—a process made harder by new visa restrictions for non-EU citizens. Historic identity and legal concerns raised For many Italian descendants abroad, this law erases more than paperwork. It threatens identity, legacy, and a deeply personal connection. Carè pointed to the emotional weight of the reform: “This identity cannot be erased. Those with Italian blood cannot be denied the right to feel part of the Republic.” Legal experts and community leaders have also raised red flags about the retroactive nature of the law. While exceptions exist for those who filed or received appointments before March 27th, 2025, others have lost eligibility overnight, even after investing years and savings into the process. What comes next for affected families Applicants now face tough decisions. Many who once dreamed of dual citizenship must consider uprooting their lives to meet Italy’s stricter demands. Others will drop their claims altogether, disheartened by the shifting landscape. Advocacy groups abroad are already organizing petitions, protests, and legal appeals. Leaders like Carè promise continued resistance “inside and outside Parliament.” (Image courtesy of tupungato via iStock) New limits alter pathways for aspirants across generations The end of citizenship claims through great-grandparents forces long-term hopefuls to reorient their plans. While short-term travelers to the EU remain unaffected, those seeking family reunification or eventual residency may face costly, uncertain routes. Migrants must now prove closer lineage—only those with at least a parent or grandparent born in Italy qualify, significantly narrowing options. This coincides with the upcoming European Travel Information and Authorization System (ETIAS) rollout, making it harder for non-EU visitors to transition from travel authorization to residency, especially under tightened Schengen visa scrutiny. Reflection of tougher migration posture Italy’s legislative pivot is emblematic of a broader EU trend toward restrictive immigration. The citizenship decree, justified under administrative and national security grounds, curtails automatic rights based on ancestry and limits retroactive claims, even for those born abroad before the law’s passage. Lawmakers positioned the move as a crackdown on “passport opportunism,” but critics argued that it alienates diasporic ties and sets a precedent for stricter heritage-based naturalization models across Europe. A wound across generations Italy’s new citizenship decree has instead become a symbolic rupture between the Republic and millions of its descendants abroad. Critics argued that it dismisses shared heritage and identity, reducing citizenship to a matter of convenience rather than connection. As families face rejection and lawmakers vow continued resistance, the legacy of jus sanguinis now hangs in the balance, fragmented, but not forgotten.
